subject: physics
title: Orbits and Kepler's Third Law
welcome_lead: Balance gravity with centripetal force to derive T² ∝ r³.
meta_desc: A-Level Gravitational Fields adventure on circular orbits and Kepler's third law.
final_note: Geostationary satellites orbit Earth in exactly 24 hours at ~42,000 km radius.

concepts.def: Passes over both poles, low altitude usual.

walkthroughs.body_html: G M m / r² = m v² / r. Cancel m, rearrange: v² = G M / r, so v = √(GM/r). Higher orbits are slower.
Substitute v = 2π r / T into v² = GM/r. Result: T² ∝ r³. Bigger orbits take much longer (cube root squared relation).
Set T = 24 h = 86,400 s, solve r ≈ 4.2 × 10⁷ m (above equator). Satellite stays above one spot on Earth — perfect for TV and weather.

mcqs.q: Higher orbital radius means orbital speed is:
When you push a wall, what does Newton's third law say about the wall?
options: The wall only pushes back if your force is strong enough to make it react.
Only when the force is small enough to be ignored.
The wall exerts an equal and opposite force on you at the same instant.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two masses doubles, what happens to the gravitational force between them?
options: It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
It halves — gravitational force is inversely proportional to distance.
It quarters — gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
